job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Ivan Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Look, my days start at six with a run along the harbour in Port Harlow, then I'm at the table in the flat I share with my brother Daniel, above my uncle's restaurant. I studied finance with a good result, and spent eight weeks at a small brokerage, Calder and Webb, where I watched how clients talk about money. I use AI every day: for research, for interview prep and for building a little model of local restaurants' costs. Afternoons I wait tables at my uncle's place, and I'm pitching to local tradesmen for bookkeeping work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the market was getting ahead of itself on this stuff. I'd tell my uncle his restaurant stays the same, and I'd tell friends that the useful tools are still useful. Online I'd say nothing, because I don't want to look like a loser who's waiting around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, flat doesn't help me. Port Harlow has maybe three finance jobs a year and I've missed them all. I'm carrying a big loan and waiting tables at my uncle's place, which is honest, but my degree isn't being used. I'm not scared of work, but I'm scared of drifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the bookkeeping idea. I've got a pitch for plumbers, electricians and restaurants, offering monthly books and tax prep for a flat fee. I'd use AI to do the grunt work so I could handle twenty clients alone. I'd also keep applying to brokerages and move to a bigger city if something real comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up, honestly. I don't do waiting. But there's a tight feeling too, because if the pitch fails I've wasted three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you price the monthly bookkeeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hundred and twenty pounds a month for a small tradesman, two-fifty for a restaurant. At twenty clients that's about three thousand a month, which beats any entry job here. Of course getting twenty clients is the hard part, so I'd start with five and use my uncle's contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if you don't get five clients in three months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I shut it down and move to the city for a job, whatever it pays, and I take on a roommate. It's a bet with a limit. I told myself I won't throw more than three months and a hundred pounds at it.

I'd tell my uncle his **restaurant** stays the same.
think: Flat doesn't help me: Port Harlow has **three finance jobs** a year.

feel: **Fired up**, with a tight feeling about wasting three months.

fieldNote: Entrepreneurial: he sets a **limit** on his bet and a price list.
Uses AI as a work multiplier, so he expects to handle many clients alone.
His fear is **drifting**, not hard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, this is where the market rewards people who move. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and sell the results, not the hours. At church I'd say we should help the older folks who'll struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's a threat and an opening at the same time. Entry jobs in finance are checking and reporting, which is exactly what software does well. But small firms can't afford big teams, and a young guy with the tools can serve many of them. That's me, if I'm fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bookkeeping to thirty clients, automate the repeat work and add services, like cash-flow forecasts and tax planning. I'd put a little money, maybe fifty a month, into an index fund and keep learning about investing. And I'd apply for jobs at firms that use AI heavily, because that's where I'd learn fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a stone of worry. It feels like the start of a race, and I like races, but I can't afford to fall in the first lap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a small firm choose you over an AI tool they can buy themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Trust and speed. A plumber doesn't want to learn software, just someone who answers the phone and says it's done. I'd be the face, and the tool does the work behind me. My uncle trusts me with his restaurant's books, and that's a real reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger brother, Daniel, who's starting a business degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, but build something while you study. Don't wait for the diploma to be useful. And don't borrow like I did without a plan, because interest eats confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if it's two years, everyone should stop pretending and get moving. I'd tell my family to save and avoid big debts. I'd say governments should not slow people down, but they should make sure families aren't wiped out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is a different game. If machines do all thinking work, finance becomes a few people with a lot of money and a lot of software. I'd be 25 with a loan and no real edge. I'd have to own something, because wages become fragile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw everything at owning assets and building clients that I keep, even if the profit is small. I'd move money into broad index funds, keep my costs very low, and push the bookkeeping hard while it's still worth something. I'd also learn a trade skill, because hands-on work lasts three years longer, and ask my uncle about a share in the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rush and a fear. I'm wired to act, so my brain says go, but my chest says you only get one shot. I'd barely sleep for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask your uncle about a share. What would that actually be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five percent, in return for taking over his accounts, his ordering and his ads. It gives me something I own that isn't a wage. He's proud, so I'd have to ask carefully, but family helps family if you show you can pull your weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031. Does the restaurant stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit longer than office jobs. But there are already robot kitchens in some cities. So I'd treat the restaurant as a three-year bridge and use it to build a second business. Owning something is the point, not the restaurant itself.

steps.text: Ask his uncle for a small share of the restaurant in return for running the accounts

Push the bookkeeping service hard for six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who move now. I'd tell friends, start something this year. I'd say society should give people room to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is a decent runway. I could get a job in a city, learn how a real firm works, and build clients on the side. By 2031 I'd have a small stake and a track record. The risk is that the window closes faster than the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best finance job I can get, even in another city, and do bookkeeping on the side. I'd invest every month and keep my costs low. I'd also use AI to do my own work faster than colleagues, so I'm the one who looks indispensable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, mostly, with sharp edges. Five years feels like a game I can play. I'd keep a list of milestones so I can tell if I'm behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What milestones are on the list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By one year: a job or ten clients. By two: loan down by a third and a first savings of a few thousand. By four: something I own, like a share in a business or a small property. If I'm behind, I change the plan, not the target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to the city even with Daniel and your uncle here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd miss them, and my uncle would grumble, but a city has hundreds of firms. I'd come home on Sundays when I could. Family is why I work, but family would also tell me to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot, and the smart ones will build something. I'd tell people to learn, save and own a piece of something. I'd also say let the young try without too many rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I like my chances. Ten years lets me qualify properly, build a business, buy a small property and still be young. The change will come, but I'd be on the right side of it, owning rather than just working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, grow my own small firm, and learn the new tools every year. I'd put aside money for a deposit and buy a small place within six or seven years. And I'd stay close to Daniel and my uncle, and probably help Daniel start his own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. It's the version where my effort pays. A small knot because I'm impatient, but mostly I'd feel like I'm in the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your firm look like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ten people, mixing accountants and AI specialists, serving small businesses across the region. Not glamorous, but steady and mine. I'd want my uncle's restaurant as client number one, with a framed invoice on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change how you'd treat the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd not rush it. I'd pay the minimum and invest the rest, since the returns over ten years should beat the interest. It's a calculated risk, and I'd review it every year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build assets or clients that last, and my debt would still be there. What would help is a fair place to start a small firm, cheap loans for young people with a plan, and trust from clients that I'm not just a kid with a laptop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable is a start, not a guarantee. The thing I'd ask for is a chance to own something, because a wage can disappear but a client or a share doesn't.

headlineQuote: A wage can disappear but a client or a share doesn't.
portrait: Ivan, 23, has a **good finance degree**, eight weeks at a brokerage and shares a flat with his brother.
He uses AI **every day**, pitches bookkeeping to tradesmen and restaurants, and waits tables for his uncle.
He favours free markets, family and **owning something**, and he sets limits and milestones.
His mood is anxious in most worlds, alarmed in 2028, and calm only with ten years.
He would move to a city, invest monthly and use **speed and trust** as his edge.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most: no time to build assets or clients that last.
whatWouldHelp: A fair place to start a small firm, **cheap loans** for young people with a plan, and client **trust**.
